absolute_simultaneity_positive: The interval of duration which separates two occurrences is a magnitude fixed in the nature of things, and cannot be altered by the motion of any observer whatsoever.
When a distant star flashes and a bell rings at the observatory, the temporal distance between these two events is an absolute quantity common to every rational mind.
It is a first principle of natural philosophy that the instant now passing at the antipodes is the very same instant here, however imperfect our means of ascertaining it.
Duration, as Newton rightly maintained, floweth equably without regard to anything external, so that a second at Greenwich is a second at Calcutta and a second upon the sun.
Were two chronometers of perfect construction placed at opposite ends of the earth, they would mark the same universal now, provided only that their errors of adjustment had been eliminated.
The propagation of light from one station to another occupies a definite interval of time, and this interval is independent of any motion which the earth may possess in the ether.
If an explosion be observed at London and a second at Edinburgh, there subsists between them a real order of succession which no change of standpoint can invert.
It belongs to the very concept of an event that it occupies a moment of universal time, and that this moment is what it is quite apart from any observer.
The comparison of physical processes carried on in distant laboratories rests upon the tacit assumption that the same absolute instant may be assigned to each.
The astronomer, in reducing his observations to a common epoch, presupposes that the epoch itself has a meaning independent of the state of motion of his instruments.
Simultaneity of two occurrences, however remote from one another in space, is a relation which inheres in the events themselves and requires no reference to a frame.
Should a signal quit the earth at a given moment and reach Mars at a later, the difference of these moments is a real interval which every intelligence must acknowledge.
The velocity of light being a constant of nature, the time required for its transit between two points is a determinate quantity, unaffected by the observer's condition of rest or motion.
The doctrine that events distant in space nevertheless share a common present is so deeply seated in reason that its denial would render astronomy itself unintelligible.
Two lightnings, one at the north pole and one at the south, either flash together or they do not, and no artifice of observation can render the question ambiguous.
The universal clock of nature ticks off its seconds without regard to any material frame, and by this clock all events, howsoever separated, may in principle be dated.
The interval elapsing between the striking of the hour at Paris and its striking at Berlin is a fact of the physical world, not a construction dependent upon the traveller.
It follows from the true theory of duration that the order of events upon the sun, could we but perceive them without delay, would agree in every particular with the order assigned by us.
The instant at which a comet reaches perihelion is one and the same for every possible observer, whether he stand upon the earth, upon Jupiter, or upon the comet itself.
That an event has taken place at a definite moment of absolute time is a proposition presupposed by every measurement, and it cannot be surrendered without dissolving the science of dynamics.
relativity_of_simultaneity_negative: Two events which appear coincident in time to an observer at rest in the ether may fail to be so for an observer borne along with the earth in her orbit.
The relation of simultaneity, as recent inquiry has shown, cannot be predicated of two separated occurrences without tacit reference to the frame in which the judgment is made.
Whether the flash at one station and the flash at another are to be reckoned contemporaneous depends upon the convention by which their clocks have been set in agreement.
The temporal coordinate assigned to a distant occurrence is not a datum of nature, but is contingent upon the state of motion of the observer who assigns it.
If we admit, as we must, that light requires time to travel from one station to another, then the very meaning of 'at the same moment' at the two stations becomes a matter of definition.
Between two events so situated that no signal could pass from one to the other, there is properly no fact as to which took place the earlier.
The synchronisation of clocks at a distance is accomplished only by a stipulation concerning the transmission of light, and simultaneity thus acquires the character of a convention.
Were the observer to change his velocity with respect to the ether, the order in which two remote events appeared to him to occur might be reversed.
It has become manifest that the presumed universal now is a phantom of the imagination, dissolving whenever we attempt to secure it by physical means.
The proposition that two distant clocks strike together has no absolute significance, but only such meaning as the mode of their comparison confers upon it.
For two events separated by an interval which no luminous ray can traverse, there exist frames of reference in which their order of occurrence is opposite to that assigned in another.
Since the transmission of any signal occupies a finite time, the affirmation that two remote events are simultaneous must always be qualified by reference to a particular observer.
The apparent time of a distant event, as recorded by a moving observer, differs from that recorded by one at rest by a quantity which depends upon their relative motion.
The judgment of simultaneity is not an immediate deliverance of experience, but is mediated by conventions concerning the propagation of light and the adjustment of clocks.
Two occurrences which the terrestrial physicist reckons as strictly contemporaneous would, to a hypothetical observer moving with great velocity, present themselves as separated in time.
It is no longer permissible to speak of the present moment of the fixed stars, save with the understanding that such a present is defined only relatively to a chosen system of reference.
The order of succession among spatially disjoined events, when the intervals are less than that required for the passage of light, is a matter upon which the choice of frame legislates.
Since our only means of coordinating distant clocks is by means of signals of finite velocity, the equality of times at separated stations rests upon a stipulation, not upon nature.
A pair of flashes deemed coincident by the stationary observer will be reported successive by the observer in rapid translation, and neither report enjoys any priority over the other.

The seeming absoluteness of the temporal order in ordinary experience arises from the smallness of terrestrial velocities compared with that of light, and vanishes so soon as this comparison is altered.
